Multiple key files can be provided, and any unused ones 174 will be ignored. "-" may be used to read identities from standard input. 175 176 When --encrypt is specified explicitly, -i can also be used to encrypt to an 177 identity file symmetrically, instead or in addition to normal recipients. 178 ``` 179 180 ### Multiple recipients 181 182 Files can be encrypted to multiple recipients by repeating `-r/--recipient`. Every recipient will be able to decrypt the file. 183 184 ``` 185 $ age -o example.jpg.age -r age1ql3z7hjy54pw3hyww5ayyfg7zqgvc7w3j2elw8zmrj2kg5sfn9aqmcac8p \ 186 -r age1lggyhqrw2nlhcxprm67z43rta597azn8gknawjehu9d9dl0jq3yqqvfafg example.jpg 187 ``` 188 189 #### Recipient files 190 191 Multiple recipients can also be listed one per line in one or more files passed with the `-R/--recipients-file` flag. 192 193 ``` 194 $ cat recipients.txt 195 # Alice 196 age1ql3z7hjy54pw3hyww5ayyfg7zqgvc7w3j2elw8zmrj2kg5sfn9aqmcac8p 197 # Bob 198 age1lggyhqrw2nlhcxprm67z43rta597azn8gknawjehu9d9dl0jq3yqqvfafg 199 $ age -R recipients.txt example.jpg > example.jpg.age 200 ``` 201 202 If the argument to `-R` (or `-i`) is `-`, the file is read from standard input. 203 204 ### Post-quantum keys 205 206 To generate hybrid post-quantum keys, which are secure against future quantum 207 computer attacks, use the `-pq` flag with `age-keygen`. This may become the 208 default in the future. 209 210 Post-quantum identities start with `AGE-SECRET-KEY-PQ-1...` and recipients with 211 `age1pq1...`. The recipients are unfortunately ~2000 characters long. 212 213 ``` 214 $ age-keygen -pq -o key.txt 215 $ age-keygen -y key.txt > recipient.txt 216 $ age -R recipient.txt example.jpg > example.jpg.age 217 $ age -d -i key.txt example.jpg.age > example.jpg 218 ``` 219 220 Support for post-quantum keys is built into age v1.3.0 and later. Alternatively, 221 the `age-plugin-pq` binary can be installed and placed in `$PATH` to add support 222 to any version and implementation of age that supports plugins. Recipients will 223 work out of the box, while identities will have to be converted to plugin 224 identities with `age-plugin-pq -identity`. 225 226 ### Passphrases 227 228 Files can be encrypted with a passphrase by using `-p/--passphrase`. By default age will automatically generate a secure passphrase. Passphrase protected files are automatically detected at decrypt time. 229 230 ``` 231 $ age -p secrets.txt > secrets.txt.age 232 Enter passphrase (leave empty to autogenerate a secure one): 233 Using the autogenerated passphrase "release-response-step-brand-wrap-ankle-pair-unusual-sword-train". 234 $ age -d secrets.txt.age > secrets.txt 235 Enter passphrase: 236 ``` 237 238 ### Passphrase-protected key files 239 240 If an identity file passed to `-i` is a passphrase encrypted age file, it will be automatically decrypted. 241 242 ``` 243 $ age-keygen | age -p > key.age 244 Public key: age1yhm4gctwfmrpz87tdslm550wrx6m79y9f2hdzt0lndjnehwj0ukqrjpyx5 245 Enter passphrase (leave empty to autogenerate a secure one): 246 Using the autogenerated passphrase "hip-roast-boring-snake-mention-east-wasp-honey-input-actress". 247 $ age -r age1yhm4gctwfmrpz87tdslm550wrx6m79y9f2hdzt0lndjnehwj0ukqrjpyx5 secrets.txt > secrets.txt.age 248 $ age -d -i key.age secrets.txt.age > secrets.txt 249 Enter passphrase for identity file "key.age": 250 ``` 251 252 Passphrase-protected identity files are not necessary for most use cases, where access to the encrypted identity file implies access to the whole system. However, they can be useful if the identity file is stored remotely. 253 254 ### SSH keys 255 256 As a convenience feature, age also supports encrypting to `ssh-rsa` and `ssh-ed25519` SSH public keys, and decrypting with the respective private key file. (`ssh-agent` is not supported.) 257 258 ``` 259 $ age -R ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub example.jpg > example.jpg.age 260 $ age -d -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 example.jpg.age > example.jpg 261 ``` 262 263 Note that SSH key support employs more complex cryptography, and embeds a public key tag in the encrypted file, making it possible to track files that are encrypted to a specific public key. 264 265 #### Encrypting to a GitHub user 266 267 Combining SSH key support and `-R`, you can easily encrypt a file to the SSH keys listed on a GitHub profile. 268 269 ``` 270 $ curl https://github.com/benjojo.keys | age -R - example.jpg > example.jpg.age 271 ``` 272 273 Keep in mind that people might not protect SSH keys long-term, since they are revokable when used only for authentication, and that SSH keys held on YubiKeys can't be used to decrypt files. 274 275 ### Inspecting encrypted files 276 277 The `age-inspect` command can display metadata about an encrypted file without decrypting it, including the recipient types, whether it uses post-quantum encryption, and the payload size. 278 279 ``` 280 $ age-inspect secrets.age 281 secrets.age is an age file, version "age-encryption.org/v1". 282 283 This file is encrypted to the following recipient types: 284 - "mlkem768x25519" 285 286 This file uses post-quantum encryption. 287 288 Size breakdown (assuming it decrypts successfully): 289 290 Header 1627 bytes 291 Encryption overhead 32 bytes 292 Payload 42 bytes 293 ------------------- 294 Total 1701 bytes 295 296 ``` 297 298 For scripting, use `--json` to get machine-readable output.
